To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
three boys with a PTPN11 mutation, T468M, had a phenotype consistent with the diagnosis of LS, and they fulfilled the NF1 diagnostic criteria, which were revised in 2017.

1) PTPN11 T468M mutation is a common cause of LEOPARD syndrome; 2) LEOPARD syndrome can present with a phenotype that fulfils the clinical criteria for diagnosis of neurofibromatiosis type 1; and 3) the diagnosis of LEOPARD should be considered in patients with hyperpigmented spots associated with hypertophic cardiopathy, even if they fulfil the clinical criteria for neurofibromatiosis type 1
the three patients with NF1 and some features of NS were actually affected with LS, and this was confirmed by the identification of a mutation in the PTPN11 (T468M) gene, which was typical of LS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the differential diagnosis of NS, NFNS, and LS.
the identification of the genetic cause of LEOPARD syndrome in three boys with neurofibromatous disease.
the clinical and genetic characterization of three patients diagnosed as having NF1 and NS, who in fact had LS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these three patients have LS, not NFNS.
these patients have a variant of LS, with some features overlapping with NS.
these three patients have LEOPARD syndrome and not NFNS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of lentigines in patients with features overlapping NS and NF1 should lead to the consideration of the possibility of LS, which is caused by mutations of the PTPN11 (protein tyrosine phosphatase, non-receptor type 11) gene.
the clinical features of the patients with NF1 and PTPN11 mutation are similar to the patients with NS and NF1, but not identical.
the diagnosis of NFNS is not a diagnosis but a diagnosis of exclusion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the clinical overlap between NFNS and LS is so great that the differential diagnosis is difficult.
the presence of multiple lentigines in patients with features overlapping with NS and NF1 should prompt LS to be considered in the differential diagnosis.
the clinical diagnosis of LS should be considered in patients with features suggestive of NF1 and NS, even when the minimal criteria for NF1 are fulfilled.
